passage:
Dear Tanuja,

You asked how the freelance job is going, so here is the honest version. The client sent back my brochure design with three lines: "Make the blue bigger. Change the font. Fine otherwise." No questions, no mention of the brief I spent a week on. I sat there feeling as if the work was invisible, and I even wondered if I am simply not good at this.

Then I remembered what you told me last spring about pinning things down. So I wrote back: "Who should the blue speak to? Can you confirm the final font and the sign-off date?" The client replied within an hour, with real answers. Nothing about my work had changed, only my questions. I will keep asking. Thank you for the nudge.

Love,
Nikita

qa.q: What did the client's message say about the brochure design?
qa.a: The client wrote "Make the blue bigger. Change the font. Fine otherwise." with no questions.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when the reply came, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nikita felt the work was invisible and even wondered about being "simply not good at this", which shows how much the short reply stung.

qa.q: What could Nikita do next time a client replies with so little?
qa.a: Ask direct questions, such as who the design should speak to and what the final font and sign-off date are, so decisions get pinned down.

qa.q: How might Tanuja read this letter?
qa.a: Tanuja may be glad that the earlier advice about pinning things down worked, and may notice that the client's silence was never a verdict on Nikita's quality.

grounding: A client barely engages with the work and Nikita moves from demoralised to asking direct questions instead of internalising the disinterest.

Gargi had spent a week writing the annual report for Santosh's logistics firm in Guindy. Twelve pages, charts, a story about their drivers. He replied in four minutes: "Looks ok. Make it more punchy." Nothing else.
The next draft got "Hmm, not sure. Try again." She could see from the shared file that he'd opened it for thirty seconds.
That night, on her balcony, she felt flat and useless. Was she just bad at this?
Then she remembered the two other clients who had praised the same style last month. The problem wasn't her writing. It was that Santosh wasn't really reading.
In the morning she sent three direct questions: "1. Which section feels least punchy? 2. Should the driver story stay, yes or no? 3. Who else needs to approve this?" She added, "A ten-minute call on Thursday would help me finish by Monday."
He replied: "Driver story yes. Call Thursday. My partner decides the rest."

qa.q: How long did Santosh have the second draft open?
qa.a: For thirty seconds, according to the shared file.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling on her balcony that night?
qa.a: She felt flat and useless, doubting whether she was simply bad at her work.

qa.q: How did Gargi respond to the client's disinterest?
qa.a: She asked three direct questions, pinned down decisions, and requested a short call, instead of taking the vague replies as a verdict on her writing.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Gargi's direct questions?
qa.a: Santosh seems too busy or distracted to engage, and the simple yes-or-no questions make it easier for him to decide.

grounding: A client barely reads the work and asks for vague changes; the protagonist asks direct questions, pins down decisions, and does not take the disinterest as a verdict.

passage:
"Aditi, did you get a chance to look at the three logo options?"
"Yeah, yeah. They're fine. Can you make them... more modern?"
Jaya kept her voice even. "Sure. Which one feels closest to modern for you?"
"I didn't really open all of them. Just pick one."
Jaya's heart sank. Three weeks of work. "I can recommend one. But it's your brand, and I want you to like it. Can I share my screen for two minutes?"
"Okay, quickly."
"Option A, or option C?"
"C. The blue."
"Great. Do you want the name in capitals or small letters?"
"Small."
"And is anyone else deciding with you?"
"My co-founder, but he trusts me."
"Perfect. I'll send C in small letters by Friday. Could you reply yes or no by Monday?"
"Yes. Fine. Thanks, Jaya."
After the call, Jaya wrote down every decision and emailed it to Aditi, just to be sure. Then she reminded herself: not reading isn't the same as not liking.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when Aditi admitted not opening all the options?
qa.a: Jaya felt her heart sink, disappointed after three weeks of work.

qa.q: How did Jaya get decisions from a disengaged client?
qa.a: She shared her screen, asked simple either-or questions, confirmed who else decides, set deadlines, and emailed the decisions afterwards.

qa.q: How might Aditi experience the quick screen-share?
qa.a: Aditi seems busy and distracted, and probably finds it easier and even relieving to make decisions when given clear choices.

grounding: A client barely engages with the work; the protagonist asks direct questions, pins down decisions in writing, and does not take the disinterest personally.
